notes.title: Chapter map: TLS

headings.text: 🌳 Decision tree: which TLS model does this hop get?

notes.html:
Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection

The section answers one question, who am I really talking to, and who else can read this? The costs are one round trip per new connection, a certificate per boundary, and a date that ends everything when it passes. Almost nothing here fails in the cipher.

Concept map

The properties come first, the handshake delivers them, and certificates carry the hard one. Termination and mTLS then decide where each property stops.

Green is CORE, blue is SUPPORTING, yellow is BREADTH, grey is a neighbouring section: TCP, QUIC, proxies and mesh.

Reading order:what TLS gives youthe TLS 1.3 handshakecertificatestermination modelsmTLSSNI, suites and automation

Owners

Idea Owner note
The three properties, what TLS doesn't give, why identity comes first what TLS gives you
Flights, key_share, HelloRetryRequest, early data, replay, handshake CPU TLS 1.3 handshake
The whole setup table: TCP, TLS, QUIC, reuse the handshake
TLS record overhead, the 22 B trace OSI and the request path
Chain, SAN, validity, revocation, verify codes certificates
ACME, HSTS, pinning, rotation breadth card
SNI and ECH SNI card
Routing on SNI without a key SNI peeking card; first named in L4 vs L7

Terminate, pass through, re-encrypt; forwarded client identity and the strip rule termination models
What else a reverse proxy does after terminating reverse proxy responsibilities
L4 and L7 products, the tradeoff table L4 vs L7 table, load balancer types; dated facts below
CertificateRequest, proof of possession, SPIFFE identity mTLS
When an API should use mTLS API authentication
A mesh's cost and when it pays service mesh
Connection reuse connection pooling

QUIC's fused handshake QUIC

Decision tree: which TLS model does this hop get?

Ask it per hop. The binding question is whether anyone may read, because a legal or contractual "no" rules out everything else. The default leaf is plain termination at a trusted edge: it's the simplest, and every other leaf has to earn its extra certificates. Termination models owns the comparison.

  • Pass-through (termination models): changes if you need a WAF or status codes; then accept a readable hop.
  • Terminate (same note): changes if a compliance rule covers internal wires; then re-encrypt.
  • mTLS (mTLS): changes if you have a handful of services and no mesh; a boundary plus tokens is cheaper.
  • Re-encrypt (termination models): changes if the backend must judge the client's certificate itself; then pass through.

At a glance

Note What it buys What it costs Who in the middle acts on it How it fails The control
What TLS gives privacy, integrity, a known peer a handshake, 22 B a record whichever hop terminates verification off, silently verification on by default
TLS 1.3 handshake setup in 1 RTT, encrypted certificate a guess; replay if 0-RTT the terminator gates early data resumption collapse, replay safe methods only, pooling
Certificates delegated, containable trust a chain to send, a date every terminating hop gap in chain, expiry date alert at the socket
Termination models L7 control where you choose keys, plaintext or a second session L7 proxy or SNI-peeking L4 box forged identity header, blind dashboards strip, per-hop model
mTLS identity from a key a certificate per workload sidecars, terminators rotation failure, plaintext accepted short lifetimes, a mesh

  • The one big idea: a proxy can act only on what it can read, and encryption means nothing without identity, so choose per hop who reads and how each side proves itself.
  • The two most-confused pairs: resumption vs 0-RTT (saves CPU and bytes, or saves a round trip and accepts replay); termination vs pass-through (ask who holds the private key).

notes.title: TLS & Transport Security — Breadth Flashcards

headings.text: Cipher suites, forward secrecy and session resumption

notes.html:
SNI

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection

One IP serves a thousand hostnames because the client names the host in the ClientHello (RFC 6066 §3), so the server can pick a certificate before keys exist. That name is therefore in clear. Encrypted Client Hello (RFC 9849) seals the real name inside and shows only public_name, usually published in an HTTPS record (RFC 9848). On a local OpenSSL 4.0.3 run, a relay read public.lab.test while the server resolved inner api.lab.test. DNS and IP addresses can still reveal it. Handshake in TLS 1.3.

SNI peeking at L4

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection

An L4 box reads the ClientHello without consuming it, takes server_name, chooses a backend, then copies bytes. It holds no key, so TLS stays end to end: nginx's ssl_preread (not built by default), Envoy's TLS inspector. A local relay routed two hostnames this way with no /v1/ visible in the forwarded bytes. Buffer past one segment, because OpenSSL's default hello was 1,472 B. Plan a default route for clients without SNI. ECH leaves only the public name. The model is in termination models.

Cipher suites, forward secrecy and session resumption

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection

A TLS 1.2 suite named everything; a 1.3 suite names only the AEAD and hash, and five exist. Forward secrecy means ephemeral key exchange, so a stolen long-term key can't open recorded traffic. Resumption uses a ticket, valid for at most 7 days, and skips certificate work. The trap is the fleet: instances must share ticket keys, or returning clients silently fall back to full handshakes. nginx uses a random key by default (Nov 2026), so set ssl_session_ticket_key across hosts. Round trips are in TLS 1.3.

HSTS, pinning, rotation and automation

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper request

HSTS (RFC 6797) makes browsers refuse plain HTTP for a host; preloading closes the first-visit gap, and hstspreload.org asks for one year, includeSubDomains and preload (Nov 2026). ⚪ HPKP (RFC 7469) is obsolete: bad pins locked sites out. Rotation means ACME (RFC 8555) over HTTP-01 or DNS-01 (§8.3, §8.4), TLS-ALPN-01 (RFC 8737), with server-suggested windows from RFC 9773. Alert on the served date, not the job. Lifetimes are in certificates.

notes.title: What TLS Gives You — Encryption, Integrity, Identity
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9846 §1: Introduction · 📜 RFC 9846 §4.5.1: Certificate · MDN: Transport Layer Security

TL;DR

TLS gives you confidentiality, integrity and identity, and people rank them backwards. Encryption is what everyone names and the part that doesn't fail. Identity is what the other two depend on: encrypting to an unverified peer is a private conversation with whoever answered.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:key agreementshared keysAEAD gives confidentiality and integritycertificate checkedidentity knownthe keys now belong to the party you meant
check skippedsame encryptionpeer unknown

Recall

Prompt Answer
The three properties? Confidentiality, integrity, authentication of the peer.
What doesn't TLS give you? Authorization, availability, protection once terminated.
Where do its round trips go? Into the handshake only; records add bytes, not round trips.

The idea

A service calls a partner over https://, and someone sets verify=False to get past a certificate error. Everything keeps working, and the cipher is as strong as before. Now an attacker on the path answers the connection with their own key, reads the token, and opens a second TLS connection to the real server. Both legs are encrypted.

So encryption alone answers the wrong question. It says nobody else can read this; only identity says who "this" is with. The two come from different machinery: one key agreement gives you confidentiality and integrity together, while identity needs a whole chain of trust.

The trade: three properties for about one round trip and 22 B a record, and the part you operate forever is identity, which is also the part that fails.

How it works

The interception from the idea, on a local run. The attacker holds a valid TLS session on each side; only the client's check tells them apart.

Nothing in the cipher differs between the branches. One if in the client decides whether the rest means anything.

Property What it stops How you get it How it fails
Confidentiality reading traffic AEAD with keys from key agreement a peer you never verified
Integrity undetected changes the AEAD tag on every record loudly: the record is refused
Identity the wrong peer certificate checks and a signature expiry, wrong name, verification off
Who in the middle acts on this a terminating proxy ends all three at itself plaintext inside that hop

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): TLS 1.3 is specified by RFC 9846, which obsoletes ⚪ RFC 8446 and ⚪ RFC 5246.
  • Changed in TLS 1.3: only AEAD ciphers remain, so the older MAC-and-encrypt choices are gone, and every key exchange is forward secret (RFC 9846 §1.3).
  • What's next and what won't change: key agreement is moving to hybrid post-quantum groups. The dependency on identity stays.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with Python 3.15 ssl on 127.0.0.1: a real server, an attacker with a self-signed certificate for the same name, and the same client twice.

-- verification off
attacker read: b'GET /balance token=s3cret'     # the secret, in clear, at the attacker
attacker read: b'balance=42'
client: TLSv1.3 TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 b'balance=42'  # looks perfect to the client
-- verification on
client refused: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED self-signed certificate
attacker: client refused TLSV1_ALERT_UNKNOWN_CA  # no request ever sent

Break it: is tampering detected, or only hidden? The byte relay flips one bit in a server record on its way through:

d = d[:20] + bytes([d[20] ^ 1]) + d[21:]   # in the relay, one bit, no key
# look for: the client aborts instead of delivering altered bytes
# naive belief predicts: garbled text reaches the application

Run on OpenSSL 4.0.3: the client stopped with decryption failed or bad record mac. That is integrity on a wire you don't trust, and a private network doesn't provide it.

Measure it

  • See it: openssl s_client -connect host:443 -servername host -verify_return_error prints Verify return code: 0 (ok) per connection; the version and suite prove encryption, the code proves identity.
  • In production: per client, the count of connections made with verification off, found by config audit since no error exists. Per record, bad record mac alerts should stay near zero.
  • Bounded by: a silently unverified peer → verification on by default in every client and proxy, a build check against verify=False, and no plaintext fallback.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: TLS gives you three things, and people rank them backwards. Confidentiality and integrity come from one key agreement and an AEAD cipher, and they essentially don't fail. Identity needs a certificate chain, and it's what breaks in production: expiry, a wrong name, verification turned off. Without identity the others are worthless, because you may have an encrypted session with an attacker.

Q · Mechanism — What does TLS actually check about the peer, and when? The client validates the certificate chain, the name and the dates, then verifies the signature in CertificateVerify, which proves the peer holds the private key. All of it sits inside the one round trip of the handshake. After that, every record is sealed with keys only those two endpoints have, so identity carries over to the whole connection.

Q · Trade-off — "We don't need TLS internally, it's a private network." What's your answer? Lead with identity, not eavesdropping. Without TLS, a service identifies callers by source address, so anything that can reach the address can act as anything else; "private" describes routing, not authentication. Integrity comes next, because proxies, sidecars and a compromised node all sit on the path. The cost that once justified skipping it was certificate handling, which a mesh now automates (mTLS). The tipping point is a few services behind one boundary, where tokens may do.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Record overhead 22 B TLS 1.3, AES-GCM; trace in the OSI note measured: Python 3.15 ssl, 1 Nov 2026
Added per record, in round trips 0 records ride existing data spec: RFC 9846 §5.2

Pitfalls

  • "HTTPS means the site is safe"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the padlock looks like a verdict on the site.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it says the connection is private, unmodified and to that name. A phishing domain with a valid certificate passes all three.
    ↳ Think instead: TLS authenticates a name, never an intention.
  • "Encryption is the main thing, identity is a detail" (a belief I held)
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "encrypted" is the word on every compliance form.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: a machine in the middle defeats unauthenticated encryption in one step, as the capture shows, so encryption's value depends on identity.
    ↳ Think instead: identity first; the cipher is the solved part.
  • Not the same: authentication vs authorization
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: a verified certificate feels like a permission.
    ↳ Difference: TLS proves who the peer is. What the peer may do is a policy decision above it.
    ↳ Think instead: a valid certificate is an input to authorization, never the result. In a mesh, every workload has one.
  • Don't disable verification to fix a connection error.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: curl -k and InsecureSkipVerify make the error vanish at once.
    ↳ What goes wrong: nothing fails afterwards, so no alert exists, and the workaround outlives the incident.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler fix: add the missing intermediate or trust the right CA.
  • Don't count TLS as protection at rest.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: "encrypted in transit" reads like encrypted everywhere.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a terminating proxy holds plaintext in memory by design, and logs and caches keep it.
    ↳ Do instead: treat each termination point as a place data is readable, and protect it separately.
  • Shelf life: the three properties are durable. Algorithms and groups change underneath them.

Connections

Path:OSI and the request pathwhat TLS gives youthe TLS 1.3 handshakecertificates
  • Builds on TCP vs UDP: TLS assumes an ordered byte stream; UDP needs DTLS or QUIC.
  • Owned elsewhere: certificates own the checks; the OSI note owns the 22 B trace.
  • Composes with mTLS: the same identity, in both directions.

notes.title: The TLS 1.3 Handshake — 1-RTT, 0-RTT, and What 1.2 Cost
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9846 §2: Protocol overview · 📜 RFC 9846 §8: 0-RTT and anti-replay · 📜 RFC 8470: Using early data in HTTP · 📜 RFC 10024: PQ/T hybrid key agreement for TLS · MDN: Transport Layer Security

TL;DR

TLS 1.3 takes one round trip because the client gambles: it sends a key share for a group it guesses the server will pick, so the server can derive keys and send its certificate in its first reply. TLS 1.2 took two, because negotiation came before key exchange. A returning client can send data in its first flight, and the price of that round trip is replay.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:① ClientHello + key_share guess② server derives keysServerHello, then encrypted certificate and Finished③ client Finished + requestresponse
wrong guessHelloRetryRequesta second ClientHelloone RTT lost

Recall

Prompt Answer
Round trips before the request leaves: 1.3, 1.2, 0-RTT? 1, 2 and 0, each on top of TCP's 1.
What buys 1.3 its round trip? A key_share in the ClientHello, sent on a guess.
What does a wrong guess cost? HelloRetryRequest: one RTT, the same as 1.2.
Why can 0-RTT data be replayed? Nothing fresh from the server reaches those keys: they come from an old ticket.
Which handshake messages travel in clear in 1.3? Only ClientHello and ServerHello; the certificate is encrypted.
Draw by hand: the 1.3 handshake, then the 0-RTT one Three flights, keys after the second; 0-RTT puts the request in the first.

The idea

A mobile client in Mumbai calls an origin 200 ms away. Each cold connection under TLS 1.2 spends 600 ms on setup before the request can leave, 200 of it on TCP and 400 on TLS. The server's work hasn't started, and no server metric sees it.

TLS 1.2 was slow by structure: the client couldn't begin key exchange until it knew the server's choice, so choosing took one round trip and exchanging took another. TLS 1.3 joins the two. The client sends a key share with its offer, a right guess gives the server everything at once, and the wait falls to one round trip. Because keys now exist after the ServerHello, the certificate travels encrypted.

The trade: one round trip saved by speculation, repaid when the guess misses; a second one saved by old keys, repaid in replay safety.

How it works

The full handshake, then a resumed one with early data. The client's second flight carries the request, so the handshake costs exactly one round trip.

④'s request is sealed with keys from the earlier session, before any fresh input from the server.

Rule What actually happens
Where the round trips go TCP takes 1, then TLS 1. HelloRetryRequest adds 1. Resumption alone saves none: it drops the certificate, not the flight. Only early data removes the round trip.
Forward secrecy Static RSA and static Diffie-Hellman are gone (RFC 9846 §1.3), so a later key leak can't decrypt recorded traffic. Early data is the exception: treat it as not forward secret (§2.3).
Replay §2.3 gives no non-replay guarantee between connections. §8 offers single-use tickets and recording ClientHellos, which limit replays without removing them from every deployment.
Who in the middle acts on this A terminator accepts or refuses early data per request and tells the origin with Early-Data: 1; the origin can answer 425 (RFC 8470 §5). L4 boxes see only the clear hellos.

Setup cost scales with distance, and the handshake owns the whole setup table:

TLS 1.2   = (1 + 2) · 200 ms = 600 ms    ← TCP + two TLS round trips
TLS 1.3   = (1 + 1) · 200 ms = 400 ms    ← the request leaves after TLS's one
1.3 0-RTT = (1 + 0) · 200 ms = 200 ms    ← TCP remains; TLS's trip is gone
edge at 20 ms: 1.3 = 2 · 20 ms = 40 ms   ← placement beats any TLS setting

Evolution

Lineage:1999 TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246)2008 TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246)2018 TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446)2026 TLS 1.3 revised (RFC 9846)2026 hybrid post-quantum groups (RFC 10024)
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): version 1.3 unchanged on the wire, now specified by RFC 9846. ⚪ RFC 8446 and ⚪ RFC 5246 are both obsoleted by it, as are RFC 5077, 6961, 7627 and 8422.
  • Changed in RFC 9846 (Jul 2026): a minor, backward-compatible revision. Key shares may not be reused between connections, TLS 1.0 and 1.1 may not be negotiated, and "master" secrets become "main". Section numbers moved: HelloRetryRequest is now §4.2.4, and Certificate §4.5.1.
  • What's next: hybrid groups make the first flight much larger, as the capture below shows. What won't change: one round trip is the floor until something reuses old keys.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with openssl s_client and s_server 4.0.3 through a 70-line Python byte relay on 127.0.0.1. The relay holds no key and logs each run of one direction as a flight; sizes are TLS records in bytes:

TLS 1.3, X25519 only
① C→S  ClientHello 232                     # key_share x25519, 32 B
② S→C  ServerHello 127, CCS 6, then 4 opaque records: 56, 892, 100, 74
③ C→S  CCS 6, Finished 74, GET 40          # the request is in flight 3

TLS 1.2                                    # no key_share
① C→S  ClientHello 214
② S→C  ServerHello 68, Certificate 870, ServerKeyExchange 120, Done 9
③ C→S  ClientKeyExchange 42, CCS 6, Finished 45
④ S→C  NewSessionTicket 191, CCS 6, Finished 45
⑤ C→S  GET 47                              # the request is in flight 5

Wrong guess: x25519 offered, server allows only P-256
① ClientHello 234 ② HelloRetryRequest 93 ③ ClientHello 267 ④ ServerHello 160, … ⑤ GET

Requesting in flight 3 against flight 5 is the 1 RTT against 2. In 1.2 the relay read Certificate 870 in clear. OpenSSL's defaults matter too: its default ClientHello was 1,472 B, because it offers X25519MLKEM768 with a 1,216 B share, and the ServerHello was 1,215 B.

Break it: does a server notice the same 0-RTT flight twice?

openssl s_server -accept 9443 -cert leaf.pem -key leaf.key -cert_chain chain.pem \
  -early_data -max_early_data 16384 -no_anti_replay
openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:9444 -sess_in s0.pem -early_data early.txt   # via the relay
python3 -c "import socket; socket.create_connection(('127.0.0.1',9443)).sendall(open('first.bin','rb').read())"
# look for: "POST /transfer amount=100" printed once per send of first.bin
# naive belief predicts: one POST, because TLS "prevents replay"

Run on OpenSSL 4.0.3: one client send plus two raw replays of the captured 561-byte flight printed the POST three times, without any session key. With the default anti-replay setting, this setup refused early data even on first use, so it didn't show a single accepted replay being stopped.

Measure it

  • See it: curl -w '%{time_connect} %{time_appconnect}': the gap per connection is TLS. openssl s_client -sess_in printing Reused confirms resumption.
  • In production: handshakes per second, full against resumed, per terminating tier; handshake CPU per connection. A falling resumed share with rising CPU means tickets stopped working.
  • Bounded by: replay of a state-changing request → accept early data only for safe methods at the edge, with 425 for the rest; handshake storms → pooling first (connection pooling).

Tech discussion

30-second answer: TLS 1.3 completes in one round trip because the client sends a key share for a guessed group, so the server derives keys and sends its certificate in the first reply. TLS 1.2 needed two. A wrong guess costs one back through HelloRetryRequest. Returning clients can send early data at zero round trips, but it can be replayed, so it's for safe requests only.

Q · Mechanism — What can an observer on the path see in a 1.3 handshake? Both hellos, so the offered versions, groups and, unless ECH is in use, the server name. From EncryptedExtensions on, including the certificate, everything is encrypted under handshake keys, so the 1.2 trick of reading the certificate off the wire is gone. The SNI card owns the remaining name leak.

Q · Trade-off — Your CDN offers 0-RTT. Do you turn it on? Only with the method gate. It removes a full round trip for returning clients, and that's real on a long path. The price is that the first flight can be recorded and resent, and the server can't always tell. So the edge accepts it for safe, idempotent requests and refuses the rest. A GET replayed wastes work; a POST /transfer replayed moves money. Decide per request, never per connection.

Q · Failure — Edge CPU climbs after a scale-out, bytes are flat and nothing errors. What ran out? CPU, spent on asymmetric crypto, because resumption collapsed. New instances didn't share the ticket key, so every returning client lost resumption and paid a full signature. Confirm by the resumed share falling while handshakes per second stay steady. Fix ticket-key distribution (resumption card). Then look at key type: on one machine here P-256 signed about 30× as fast as RSA-2048.

Q · Design — Design TLS for a global API where time to first byte is the product metric. Distance binds, so end TCP and TLS at an edge near the user: 2 RTT at 20 ms instead of 200 ms. Keep a warm pool from edge to origin, which pays the long leg once (termination models). Serve TLS 1.3 with an ECDSA certificate, share ticket keys across the fleet, and allow 0-RTT for safe methods only. Offer HTTP/3 with a TCP fallback (QUIC). Watch the resumed share first. The service view is in communication patterns.

Compare

Measured in the capture above, counting the client flight that carries the request:

Setup Request in flight TLS round trips Certificate sent? When you'd pick it
1.3 full 3 1 yes, encrypted the default
1.3, wrong guess 5 2 yes, encrypted never on purpose; offer common groups
1.3 resumed 3 1 no; flight 2 fell from 1,255 to 269 B returning clients
1.3 0-RTT 1 0 no safe requests on long paths
1.2 full 5 2 yes, in clear legacy clients only

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
TLS 1.3 cipher suites 5 name only the AEAD and hash spec: RFC 9846 Appendix B.4
Ticket lifetime ≤ 7 days 604,800 s; clients must stop too spec: RFC 9846 §4.7.1
ClientHello, OpenSSL defaults 1,472 B above a 1,460 B MSS, so two segments measured: OpenSSL 4.0.3, 1 Nov 2026; MSS from MTU
Signatures per second, one process P-256 90,652; RSA-2048 3,040 about 30× measured: openssl speed -seconds 1, 4.0.3, 1 Nov 2026

Pitfalls

  • "TLS 1.3 is faster because its cryptography is faster"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: new version, new ciphers, lower latency.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: the saving is one round trip from a restructured exchange. A 200 ms path saves 200 ms on any cipher.
    ↳ Think instead: count flights, not cycles. The speculative key_share is the mechanism.
  • "TLS prevents replay, so 0-RTT is just a faster handshake"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: 1-RTT data can't be replayed, and resumption feels like a shortcut through the same thing.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: early data doesn't depend on the ServerHello, so nothing fresh binds it. Three identical POSTs reached the server from one captured flight above.
    ↳ Think instead: 0-RTT is a per-request decision, gated on safe methods.
  • Not the same: resumption vs 0-RTT
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both use a ticket, and both are sold as faster reconnects.
    ↳ Difference: resumption skips certificate work but still takes the round trip. Early data removes the round trip and accepts replay.
    ↳ Think instead: resumption saves CPU and bytes; 0-RTT saves time. Each is its own choice.
  • Don't tune ciphers on a slow TLS path.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: cipher lists are visible, and a config change feels like progress.
    ↳ What goes wrong: bulk encryption isn't where the time goes, so setup latency stays exactly where it was.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler fix: reuse connections, then terminate closer, then resume, then change key type.
  • Don't assume "1.3 is one round trip" in a capacity plan.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the headline, and it's usually true.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a server restricted to a group clients don't guess adds an RTT to every handshake, which looks like a bimodal time_appconnect.
    ↳ Do instead: check for HelloRetryRequest in a capture when handshake times cluster at double.
  • Shelf life: round-trip counts are durable. Hybrid group sizes and defaults are moving, and vendor 0-RTT defaults belong to the chapter map's Landscape.

Connections

Path:what TLS gives youTLS 1.3 handshakecertificatestermination models
  • Builds on the TCP handshake: TLS starts after it, and that note owns the whole setup table.
  • Owned elsewhere: OSI and the request path owns the 22 B record trace; breadth cards own cipher suites and ticket keys.
  • Contrasts with QUIC: the same handshake fused into the transport.
  • Bounded by connection pooling: a reused connection pays nothing here.
  • Measured by where latency goes and curl mastery.

notes.title: Certificates & Chains of Trust
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 5280 §6: Path validation · 📜 RFC 9525: Service identity in TLS · 📜 RFC 9846 §4.5.1: Certificate · CA/Browser Forum: Baseline Requirements

TL;DR

Trust is delegated down a chain: a root in the client's store signs an intermediate, which signs your leaf. The server must send the leaf and the intermediates, and the client walks up to a root it already has. Validity is a hard edge with no grace period, so expiry takes everything at once, and the fix is short lifetimes plus alerts on the date.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:server sends leaf + intermediateclient checks each signature upwardroot found in its storedates checkedname matched against the SANCertificateVerify proves the key

Recall

Prompt Answer
What must the server send? Leaf and intermediates. The root is in the client's store.
Which field matches the hostname? The Subject Alternative Name; RFC 9525 forbids the Common Name.
What's the longest public certificate since 15 Mar 2026? 200 days, falling to 100 and then 47.

The idea

A team renews a certificate and deploys only the leaf. Their browser test passes, because the browser has met that intermediate before. An hour later a Python partner reports unable to get local issuer certificate, while the server's dashboards are clean. Nothing is expired and no cipher is wrong: the chain has a gap.

Chains exist because a root key is too valuable to use. Roots sit in device stores that update slowly, so a compromised root can't practically be withdrawn; the root stays offline and signs intermediates, which do the daily issuing and can be replaced. The cost of that containment is that the client lacks the middle link, so your server has to send it.

The trade: containment of a CA compromise, paid for with a chain every server must present correctly and a date that ends every connection when it passes.

How it works

Validation walks up from the leaf. Only the root is trusted in advance, and everything else is proved from it.

The root is purple because you don't run it, and it's the only box the client didn't get from your server.

Rule What actually happens
Missing intermediate Behaviour splits by client. Firefox doesn't chase AIA, but it caches and preloads intermediates; OpenSSL used only what the server sent. A browser pass proves little.
Name RFC 9525 says the Common Name must not identify a service. Browsers follow that, yet OpenSSL 4.0.3 and Python 3.15 accepted a CN-only leaf here. Issue SANs regardless.
Revocation CRLs and OCSP exist, but short lifetimes do most of the work now. Baseline Requirements made OCSP optional, and Let's Encrypt turned its OCSP off on 6 Aug 2025.
Where the round trips go None added: the chain rides the server's flight. Its size is bytes in that flight, 892 B for two small P-256 certificates here.
Who in the middle acts on this Every terminating hop holds its own certificate and date, so each termination point is one more expiry.

Evolution

Lineage:2008 PKIX profile (RFC 5280)2019 ACME (RFC 8555)2023 service identity (RFC 9525, obsoletes ⚪ RFC 6125)2025 Let's Encrypt ends OCSP2026 200-day public maximum
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the model is settled, and lifetimes are moving fast.
  • Changed in Baseline Requirements (15 Mar 2026): the maximum fell from 398 to 200 days, so an annual manual renewal is no longer possible for public certificates.
  • What's next and what won't change: 100 days on 15 Mar 2027, 47 on 15 Mar 2029. Trust remains delegation from a preinstalled root.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with openssl s_server and s_client 4.0.3 on 127.0.0.1, against a lab root, intermediate and leaf:

openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:9443 -servername api.lab.test -CAfile root.pem \
  -verify_return_error -verify_hostname api.lab.test </dev/null
# leaf + intermediate   → Verify return code: 0 (ok)
# leaf only             → 20 (unable to get local issuer certificate)
# expired leaf          → 10 (certificate has expired)
# -verify_hostname other.lab.test → 62 (hostname mismatch)
# rogue self-signed, same name    → 18 (self-signed certificate)

Each failure is a different line of an outage ticket, and the code names which check failed. One result went against the expected story: a leaf with no SAN and a matching Common Name returned 0 (ok), so don't rely on these libraries to catch it.

Measure it

  • See it: openssl s_client -showcerts lists what the server really sends; correct is leaf then intermediates, per connection. openssl x509 -noout -dates gives the window.
  • In production: days until expiry per certificate, per terminating hop, probed from outside; ACME failure counts per domain. A renewal job's own success metric doesn't count.
  • Bounded by: a total outage at notAfter → an alert on the served certificate's date with weeks of margin, staggered renewal, and a tested manual path.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: A root in the client's store signs an intermediate, which signs your leaf. The server sends the leaf and intermediates, and the client walks up to its root, checking signatures, dates and the name in the SAN. Leave out the intermediate and browsers may hide it while other clients fail. Expiry has no grace period, which is why lifetimes keep shrinking and alerts watch the date.

Q · Mechanism — Why does a missing intermediate fail in Python but pass in a browser? The server's chain has a gap, and each client fills it differently. A browser may already hold the intermediate from an earlier site or a preloaded set. OpenSSL here built the chain from what the server sent plus its trust store, and failed with code 20. So test with openssl s_client -showcerts, and read the chain rather than the padlock.

Q · Trade-off — Shorter lifetimes mean more renewals. Why accept that? Because revocation is weak and expiry isn't. A leaked key on a short certificate stops working soon with no client needing to check anything, and frequent renewal exercises the automation so it can't rot. The cost is that manual renewal stops being viable: at 47 days a human process fails. Below some size, a managed certificate on your load balancer removes the work. Above it, you need ACME and an inventory.

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Public maximum 200 days issued since 15 Mar 2026 default (as of Nov 2026): Baseline Requirements 2.3.1
Next steps 100, then 47 days 15 Mar 2027, 15 Mar 2029 same; ballot SC-081v3

Pitfalls

  • "It works in my browser, so the chain is fine"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the browser is the nearest client, and it shows a padlock.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: browsers can supply a missing intermediate from elsewhere. Service clients often can't, so the same server fails for them.
    ↳ Think instead: test the chain the server sends, with openssl s_client -showcerts.
  • "Short lifetimes are an automation convenience" (a belief I held)
    ↳ Why it's tempting: they arrived with ACME, so they look like its side effect.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: revocation checks are unreliable, so a certificate that ends soon is the containment.
    ↳ Think instead: expiry does revocation's job.
  • Not the same: renewed vs deployed
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: the renewal job reports success, so the task looks finished.
    ↳ Difference: a new file on disk protects nothing until every terminating process serves it, and a job that stopped running reports no failure at all.
    ↳ Think instead: measure the certificate served at the socket, not the job.
  • Don't watch only your own leaf.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the only date you control.
    ↳ What goes wrong: roots expire too. DST Root CA X3 expired on 30 Sep 2021, and OpenSSL 1.0.x clients failed on Let's Encrypt's Android-compatible chain although they trusted the newer root.
    ↳ Do instead: know your client population's trust stores before changing chains.
  • Shelf life: path validation is durable. Lifetimes, revocation practice and CA profiles are not: see the chapter map's Landscape.

Connections

Path:the TLS 1.3 handshakecertificatestermination modelsmTLS
  • Builds on what TLS gives you: identity is what this machinery exists for.
  • Owned elsewhere: the breadth card owns ACME, rotation and pinning.
  • Used by mTLS: the same checks against an internal CA.

notes.title: TLS Termination vs Pass-Through vs Re-encryption
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9846 §2: Protocol overview · 📜 RFC 6066 §3: Server Name Indication · nginx: ngx_stream_ssl_preread_module · Envoy: HTTP header manipulation · AWS: ALB target groups

TL;DR

A proxy can act only on what it can read, and TLS decides what it can read. Terminate and it reads everything, with plaintext behind it. Pass through and it reads nothing but the hello. Re-encrypt and it reads everything with both wires encrypted. The model is chosen per hop, and each choice names what you agree to be blind to.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverdesign time
Flow:client TLS reaches the hopproxy decrypts, routes on pathplaintext to backend
proxy peeks at SNIsame TLS session to backend
proxy decrypts, actsnew verified TLS session to backend

Recall

Prompt Answer
What does pass-through cost? Every L7 decision: path, headers, per-request balance, status metrics.
What can an L4 box still route on? SNI, while the hello is in clear; never the path.
Where does a client certificate stop? At the terminator. Past it, identity is a header.
Handshakes at re-encrypt for 5 client connections, pooled upstream? 5 at the edge, 1 to the backend, measured here.
Who holds certificates in each model? Terminate: edge. Pass-through: backend. Re-encrypt: both.
Draw by hand: the three models, side by side Client, proxy, backend; mark which wire is plain, and where keys sit.

The idea

A team fronts a payments API with a TCP load balancer so that "nothing decrypts in the middle". Then the WAF requirement arrives, and the box can't see a path. At the first incident the dashboard shows connections and bytes, with no status codes. Their security decision has quietly become an observability decision.

Move the boundary and the capability set moves with it. An L7 hop needs the request, so it must end TLS and hold a key; the wire behind it is then plaintext unless it opens a second session. Everything else follows from where encryption stops relative to where a decision is made.

The trade: visibility and control at the hop, paid in key custody, one more certificate per boundary, and a point where data sits in clear in memory.

How it works

The same request in each model. Red marks a backend reached in plaintext; yellow boxes are the hops you configure, and "key" says who can read.

Only pass-through keeps a single session from client to backend. Re-encrypted traffic is encrypted on every wire and readable inside the proxy.

Rule What actually happens
Where the round trips go Terminate puts the client's handshake at the hop, so a nearby edge shortens it. Pass-through leaves it at the backend. Re-encrypt adds a backend handshake, paid once per pooled connection.
Client identity A client certificate proves itself to whoever ends TLS, and the session ends there. Past it, the terminator asserts identity in a header (mTLS owns the handshake).
Header trust The backend now trusts text, so the terminator must overwrite any inbound copy. Envoy sanitizes X-Forwarded-Client-Cert when forward_client_cert_details is unset (Nov 2026).
Who in the middle acts on this Each model sets it: an L7 proxy decides per request; an L4 box peeks at SNI and then copies bytes it can't read.

Evolution

Lineage:2011 SNI in its current form (RFC 6066)2018 TLS 1.3 encrypts the certificate (RFC 8446)2019 ACME automates issuance (RFC 8555)2026 RFC 9849 encrypts the inner hello2026 RFC 9846 revises TLS 1.3
  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): cloud balancers expose all three as product choices (load balancer types).
  • Changed in RFC 9849 (Mar 2026): with ECH, an L4 box without the ECH key sees only the outer public name, so routing on the real hostname moves to the client-facing server that holds that key.
  • What's next and what won't change: the hello keeps shrinking as a source of information. The rule stays: to act on a request, you must read it.

On the wire

Re-encryption in nginx, annotated. nginx wasn't available here, so the config comes from its documentation, and the behaviour below comes from a Python model of each hop.

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    ssl_certificate         /etc/ssl/public.crt;     # the public CA's leaf
    ssl_certificate_key     /etc/ssl/public.key;
    ssl_client_certificate  /etc/ssl/clients-ca.crt; # ssl_verify_client needs a CA to check against
    ssl_verify_client       on;                      # off by default
    location / {
        proxy_pass https://backend;                  # https: a second TLS session
        proxy_ssl_verify on;                         # default off: encryption, no authentication
        proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/ssl/internal-ca.crt;
        proxy_ssl_server_name on;                    # default off: no SNI sent upstream
        proxy_ssl_name backend.internal;             # the name to verify
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Client-Cert $ssl_client_escaped_cert;  # redefines, never appends
    }
}

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 with Python 3.15 ssl on 127.0.0.1. The L4 box holds no key:

PASS-THROUGH  L4 box: SNI=api.lab.test -> port 9471
  backend: tls=TLSv1.3 peercert=spiffe://lab.test/ns/prod/sa/payments path=/v1/orders
  L4 box: forwarded 2675 B; b'/v1/' in them: False
RE-ENCRYPT    5 client connections, pooled upstream
  edge handshakes 5   backend handshakes 1

The client's certificate reached the backend only through the box that held no key. The pooled leg cost one handshake in six, which is why 2× is a per-connection worst case and not a latency figure.

Break it: the terminator forwards identity in a header, and a client sends that header itself.

F = b"X-Forwarded-Client-Cert: URI=spiffe://lab.test/ns/prod/sa/admin\r\n"
call(no_strip_proxy, "/x", F)                  # client holds no certificate at all
call(strip_proxy,    "/x", F)
call(strip_proxy,    "/x", F, cert=True)       # real certificate, sa/payments
# look for: the first call reaching the backend as sa/admin
# naive belief predicts: "none", because the client presented no certificate

Run on Python 3.15: admin, then none, then payments. One missing strip turned a client with no certificate into any identity it asked for.

Measure it

  • See it: openssl s_client -connect lb:443 -servername host -showcerts shows whose certificate answers; the issuer tells you which hop terminates, per connection.
  • In production: per hop, connections and bytes for pass-through; status and latency per route for terminate. Also unverified upstream connections per hop: above zero means proxy_ssl_verify was relaxed.
  • Bounded by: a forged identity header → strip at the first trusted hop and a test that sends one; an unverified upstream → verification on, with an internal CA; expiry at any hop → date alerts per termination point.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Every proxy hop has three choices. Terminate, and it reads the request at the cost of a plaintext hop. Pass through, and it forwards bytes it can't read, keeping end-to-end encryption and losing all L7 control, though it can still route on SNI. Re-encrypt, and it reads the request and opens a new TLS session. The question is what you're willing to be blind to, per hop.

Q · Mechanism — What can a load balancer do without decrypting? It sees addresses, ports, connection state and byte counts, so it balances connections, health-checks TCP and limits by source. It can peek at the ClientHello and route on SNI, and my relay did exactly that with no key. It can't read a path: the forwarded bytes held no /v1/. No per-request balancing, no status codes, no WAF. ECH removes even the inner hostname from view.

Q · Trade-off — A regulated client says "no plaintext anywhere in your infrastructure". What do you build? Ask what "anywhere" means. If it means no plaintext on a wire, re-encrypt at each hop: the WAF still works and links stay encrypted. If it means no intermediary may read, only pass-through satisfies it, and you lose edge inspection. Re-encrypting without verifying the backend's certificate satisfies the checkbox and authenticates nobody. As of Nov 2026 an ALB doesn't validate target certificates, relying on VPC packet authentication instead, so name that in the review.

Q · Failure — One tenant is down at your multi-tenant edge, and aggregate error rate barely moved. What ran out? A certificate's validity. One tenant's renewal failed silently, perhaps a DNS challenge after a nameserver change, and that domain now fails every handshake while everything else stays healthy, so the aggregate SLO hides it. Confirm with openssl s_client -servername tenant.example reading its dates. Fix by reissuing, then alert per certificate on days to expiry rather than on job success. The automation card owns renewal.

Q · Design — Design TLS for a payments API: internet clients, a WAF, services that must mutually authenticate. Two requirements pull apart: the WAF must read, and services must authenticate each other, so one model can't do it. Edge terminates with the public certificate and runs the WAF, re-encrypts to the gateway against an internal CA, and services use mTLS from a mesh. Keep public and internal trust separate. Strip identity headers at the edge. Watch expiry at all three tiers first, then unverified connections. The service view is in communication patterns.

Compare

Terminate Pass-through Re-encrypt
Backend wire plaintext the client's session new session
Routing path, header, method SNI only path, header, method
Client cert reaches backend as a header yes, in the handshake as a header
Handshakes at proxy client side none client side + pooled backend
Certificates edge backends both
When you'd pick it public web in a trusted boundary no intermediary may read L7 needs, no plaintext on wires

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Sessions per client connection 1, 1, 2 terminate, pass-through, re-encrypt spec: RFC 9846 §2
Crypto work per connection, unpooled ≈ 2× at re-encrypt two handshakes, two record streams derived
Backend handshakes for 5 client connections 1 one pooled upstream measured: Python 3.15 ssl, 1 Nov 2026
/v1/ in 2,675 B at the L4 box 0 matches pass-through, TLS 1.3 measured, same run

Pitfalls

  • "Re-encryption is end-to-end encryption"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: every wire is encrypted, and the diagram has no plaintext arrow.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: two sessions meet inside the proxy, where data is in clear in memory. Only pass-through keeps one session.
    ↳ Think instead: say "encrypted on every hop, readable at the proxy".
  • "Re-encryption doubles latency"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: two handshakes sounds like twice the cost.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: 2× is per connection and per unpooled handshake. With a pool, five client connections cost one backend handshake here.
    ↳ Think instead: separate crypto per connection from latency per request.
  • Not the same: termination vs passthrough
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both are "TLS at the load balancer", and a listener picks between them with one word.
    ↳ Difference: a TLS listener decrypts; a TCP listener on 443 forwards. As of Nov 2026, that's AWS NLB's split.
    ↳ Think instead: ask who holds the private key. That hop terminates.
  • Don't forward identity without stripping the inbound copy.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: adding the header feels complete, and tests with honest clients pass.
    ↳ What goes wrong: a client sets the header itself and becomes anyone, as the Break it shows.
    ↳ Do instead: overwrite at the first trusted hop, and test with a forged header.
  • Don't pass through just to feel safer.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: no decryption in the middle sounds strictly better.
    ↳ What goes wrong: you lose status codes, path rules and WAF, and the backend inherits certificate work it may not automate.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option: terminate at a trusted edge unless a named requirement forbids reading.
  • Shelf life: the three models are durable. Product behaviour changes: see the chapter map's Landscape.

Connections

Path:certificatestermination modelsmTLSreverse proxy responsibilities
  • Builds on L4 vs L7: pass-through is L4, and terminating is what makes L7 possible.
  • Owned elsewhere: the tradeoff table owns products; service mesh owns sidecar re-encryption's cost.
  • Composes with connection pooling: it amortises the backend handshake.
  • Bounded by certificate automation: each boundary is one more date.
  • Decided in communication patterns: where a service boundary picks its transport security.

notes.title: mTLS — Mutual Authentication and Service-Mesh Zero Trust
notes.html:
References

📜 RFC 9846 §4.4.2: Certificate Request · 📜 RFC 9846 §4.5.2: Certificate Verify · SPIFFE: X.509-SVID · Linkerd: automatic mTLS

TL;DR

Ordinary TLS proves the server to the client; mTLS adds the reverse. The server asks for a certificate, and the client sends one plus a signature proving it holds the key. Identity stops being "came from this subnet" and becomes "proved it is payments". The handshake is the easy part; issuing and rotating a certificate for every workload is the product.

Stage:resolverouteconnectsecurebalanceframemessagecontractserverecoverper connection
Flow:server sends CertificateRequest in its flightclient validates the serversends its Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finishedserver checks chain and signatureidentity bound to the connection
no certificateclient's handshake call returnscertificate_required at the first read

Recall

Prompt Answer
Which messages does mTLS add? CertificateRequest from the server; Certificate and CertificateVerify from the client.
Extra round trips? None: same four flights, measured, with about 1 KB more.
Which CA should sign workload certificates? Your own internal CA, not a public one.

The idea

Service B accepts calls from 10.0.3.0/24, because that's where service A runs. Then a compromised pod lands in that subnet, and every call it makes is "from A". The address says where a packet came from, and nothing about who sent it.

mTLS moves the question to a key. A's private key never leaves A, and it signs the handshake transcript, so a captured connection gives an attacker a public certificate and nothing to reuse. A bearer token works the other way: whoever holds the string is believed.

The trade: no round trips and very little CPU per pooled connection, and in exchange every workload needs a certificate, a key and a rotation story.

How it works

The same flights as a normal handshake, with three more messages inside them. Only the server's request and the client's two replies are new.

A learns of a refusal only in ④, after it has finished its side. That ordering is what the Break it shows.

Rule What actually happens
Proof of possession CertificateVerify signs the transcript. Without it, a certificate proves nothing, because certificates are public.
Where the round trips go Nowhere new: CertificateRequest rides flight 2, the client's messages ride flight 3.
Identity format A workload has no stable hostname, so meshes name it with a SPIFFE ID, carried as exactly one URI SAN.
Who in the middle acts on this A terminating proxy consumes the client's certificate; past it, the backend sees a header. Sidecars end mTLS for the app.

Evolution

  • Maturity: 🟢 Established (Nov 2026): the mesh default. Linkerd issues 24-hour certificates; Istio's agent requests 24 h and rotates at half.
  • Changed in Chrome Root Program 1.8 (Feb 2026): public hierarchies are moving to server authentication only, and Let's Encrypt finished removing the client-auth EKU on 8 Jul 2026. Public certificates are no longer a path to client identity.
  • What's next and what won't change: workload identity spreads to agent egress (egress security). Certificates still prove who, never what.

On the wire

Captured on 1 Nov 2026 through the byte relay on 127.0.0.1, OpenSSL 4.0.3, TLS 1.3, client certificate on (compare the plain run in the handshake note):

① C→S  ClientHello 232
② S→C  ServerHello 127, CCS 6, opaque 56, 106, 892, 101, 74   # 106 is the extra CertificateRequest
③ C→S  CCS 6, opaque 912, 101, 74, 40                         # client Certificate, Verify, Finished, GET

Still flight 3 for the request. The cost is 106 B from the server and 1,013 B from the client. A Python server in the same lab read spiffe://lab.test/ns/prod/sa/payments from the peer certificate.

Break it: does a client with no certificate fail at connect? Python 3.15 ssl, server with CERT_REQUIRED:

s = ctx.wrap_socket(socket.create_connection(addr), server_hostname="api.lab.test")
print("wrap_socket returned", s.version())    # the "connect" step
s.recv(10)                                    # the first read
# look for: where the exception appears
# naive belief predicts: wrap_socket raises, so connect logic catches it

Run: wrap_socket returned TLSv1.3, then the first read raised TLSV13_ALERT_CERTIFICATE_REQUIRED. TLS 1.3 clients finish before the server judges them, so a rejected client looks connected until it reads. A health check that stops at connect passes.

Measure it

  • See it: openssl s_client -cert client.pem -key client.key printing Acceptable client certificate CA names shows the request; correct is a response, not an alert, per connection.
  • In production: per workload, certificate time to expiry and rotation failures; connections accepted in plaintext per service. Linkerd accepts plaintext from unmeshed sources by default (Nov 2026).
  • Bounded by: a leaked key → lifetimes of hours, so it expires quickly; a CA outage stalling issuance → rotate at half life, leaving time to recover before expiry.

Tech discussion

30-second answer: Ordinary TLS authenticates the server. mTLS adds a CertificateRequest, and the client answers with a certificate and a signature over the transcript, which proves it holds the key. That replaces network position with cryptographic identity, the basis of zero trust. It adds no round trips. The hard part is issuing and rotating certificates for every workload, which is what a mesh really sells.

Q · Mechanism — What does mTLS add over TLS plus a bearer token? The credential can't be replayed from a capture: the key never travels, while a token is the secret itself. And it's enforced at transport, so an unauthenticated peer is refused before application code sees a byte, whatever language the service uses. But identity is per connection and names the workload, not the end user. So real systems run both; API authentication owns that choice.

Q · Trade-off — mTLS everywhere sounds right. When isn't it worth it? The crypto is negligible on pooled connections. The cost is lifecycle: a pod that lives minutes needs a certificate at start, and a scale-out needs many at once. In practice mTLS means adopting a mesh or an issuing system, with its own control plane and failures that look like network faults. With six services and no mesh, a guarded boundary plus tokens gives most of the benefit. Past the point where addresses stop meaning identity, it pays (service mesh).

Compare

Approach Proves A capture gives an attacker Enforced When you'd pick it
Source IP network position nothing needed network coarse tiering, never identity
Bearer token possession of a string the credential app or gateway user identity, partners
mTLS possession of a key a public certificate transport service to service
mTLS + token workload and user a token, for its lifetime both most real systems

Numbers

Number Value Context Source
Mesh certificate lifetime 24 h Linkerd; Istio agent's SECRET_TTL, grace ratio 0.5 default (as of Nov 2026): Linkerd, Istio

Pitfalls

  • "mTLS gives us zero trust"
    ↳ Why it's tempting: it's the headline feature of every mesh.
    ↳ Why it's wrong: it supplies identity. Zero trust also needs a policy per service, and without one every workload with a certificate reaches everything.
    ↳ Think instead: mTLS removes position as a credential, the first step and not the whole design.
  • Not the same: workload identity vs user identity
    ↳ Why they get mixed up: both arrive as "who is calling".
    ↳ Difference: mTLS names the calling service. It can't say which user that service acts for.
    ↳ Think instead: mTLS for the workload, a token for the user, both checked.
  • Don't plan client auth on public certificates.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: a public CA is free and already automated.
    ↳ What goes wrong: Let's Encrypt no longer issues the client-auth EKU, and trusting public roots would accept any certificate those CAs issue.
    ↳ Do instead: run a private CA, trusted only by your own services.
  • Don't hand-roll this across many services.
    ↳ Why it's tempting: the handshake config is ten lines.
    ↳ What goes wrong: rotation under ephemeral workloads becomes outages that look like network faults.
    ↳ Do instead: the simpler option below a handful of services: a boundary plus tokens; above it, a mesh or issuing system.
  • Shelf life: the handshake is durable. Mesh defaults and root-program rules are volatile: see the chapter map's Landscape.

Connections

Path:termination modelsmTLSservice mesh
  • Builds on certificates: the same checks, against an internal CA.
  • Owned elsewhere: API authentication owns when to use it for an API; service mesh owns the mesh's cost.
  • Breaks when combined with a terminating proxy: the certificate stops there.
  • Used by egress security: workload identity on outbound agent calls.
